whatItFakes: A counted member's marital status and which relative is their child: a woman is married when an adult relative within the minimum parent age of her age lives in her household, and a mother when a relative under 5 is at least that much younger.
why: The counts keep family pairs without their kind and carry no marital status, so the web's mothers and married-women outcomes cannot read a counted woman's own record.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Counted members' partner and parent-child links kept in the counts, read in place of the age rule.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: Local immigration enforcement (enforcement-to-undocumented-employment, enforcement-to-us-born-employment) reaches workers through the jobs engine's pull to work, by a work authorization seeded on who each noncitizen is (isUnauthorized in src/core2/citizenship.ts), at one national share of noncitizens who are unauthorized (parameter unauthorizedShareOfNoncitizens, Pew 2024) rather than each state's. Citizens stand for the U.S.-born the research measures, since the core records no birthplace, so naturalized citizens take the U.S.-born effect. Only the pull to work reads it; no employer checks authorization at hire.
why: Pew publishes the unauthorized population by state but no table here holds each state's noncitizens to divide it by, and people are generated without a birthplace.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A per-state unauthorized share of noncitizens (Pew state estimates over ACS noncitizens, table B05001) in place data, and a seeded nativity on people (full and counted) so naturalized citizens are told from the U.S.-born.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: The minimum-wage-to-low-wage-jobs link needs the minimum wage as a share of the place's median wage (labor.minimum-wage-to-median), which no engine records.
why: The wage floor is read by the jobs engine for pay, but the ratio to the median is not a kept measure.
replacement: A reader in the jobs engine of the wage floor over the place's median hourly pay, added to the engine measures.
resolution: gov-measures.ts records labor.minimum-wage-to-median (the governing minimum wage over the median hourly pay of the town's current jobs), and the web's model counts government measures as causes (src/core2/gov-measure-keys.ts), so minimum-wage-to-low-wage-jobs runs. Its reach to employers is SG-LABOR-low-wage-unreviewed's.

whatItFakes: Birth-year pollution (birth-year-pollution-to-adult-earnings), teacher quality (teacher-quality-to-earnings) and neighborhood years (neighborhood-years-to-adult-outcomes) acting on adult earnings move nothing, each for its own missing piece. Birth-year pollution: the exposure is on record for anyone born in play (a person:birth fact with place and date, src/core2/births-people.ts, and the web's month rows of env.particulates for that place), but no pay decision reads it and the link has no size. Teacher quality: nothing records a teacher's value-added or which teacher a student has, and no law or engine moves teacher value-added, so the cause has no producer and no policy to carry. Neighborhood years: where each person lived each year is on record (residenceOn in src/core2/past-moves.ts, and moves in play), but no data row holds a county's childhood exposure effect, no pay decision reads it and the link has no size.
why: The links are person-level (exposure-years shape): a place rate would apply them to the wrong people, so each must be read from the person's own history when pay is set.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Birth-year pollution: a read in src/core2/jobs-web.ts of the person's birth fact and the web's particulates over their birth year, sized from its study. Teacher quality: parked until a researched link moves teacher value-added (a teacher-pay or evaluation law); then the school engine keeps a value-added per teacher and a yearly classroom, and hirePay reads its mean. Neighborhood years: a county row of childhood exposure effects, read in hirePay from residenceOn and in-play moves.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: Transit loss to unemployment (transit-loss-to-unemployment), broadband to employment (broadband-to-employment), incentive deals to industry jobs (incentive-deal-to-industry-jobs) and more immigrants to the workforce (more-immigration-to-workforce) have no researched size the game can use, and a Medicaid work requirement's effect on employment (work-requirement-to-employment) is about zero, so an engine would multiply by one.
why: Their sources give a study-unit effect (one lost line, a county gaining broadband, one deal) that no conversion turns into the game's slopes; the sizes are to confirm.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Sizes confirmed from the sources and the cause measures (transit access, deal records) recorded by their engines.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: Pretrial detention lowering the pull to formal work (pretrial-detention-to-employment): the jobs engine adds the log of one plus the row's size to the choice score of anyone the justice engine first held while they waited for a hearing, from the row's lag on and for good. The research measures the gap three to four years after the hearing, not how long it lasts or whether a second detention adds to it, and every job the jobs engine keeps stands for formal employment because it keeps no informal work. A counted member carries no term: the justice engine files counted defendants as cases by group (CountedCaseRow, detained as a count), and the counts keep no record of which member was held.
why: Dobbie, Goldin and Yang (2018) compare formal employment three to four years after the bail hearing; the game has no informal work to set it against, and the counted tier's detention is a head count per case, not a record of a member the jobs engine could read.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A duration from the research on the term; a record of which counted member was held, for the counted tier to read as a named person's is; and the term fitted in a played year so detained defendants' share at work runs the researched 20% under that of those released (see SG-LABOR-participation-scale).
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: The size of the web's participation effects on mothers and married women at work, and of the pull to formal work of anyone the justice engine first held while they waited for a hearing (pretrial-detention-to-employment): the engine adds the log of the factor to a deterministic choice score, which reaches the records but is not fitted to the researched size. The older workers' term has its own fitted weight (jobsOlderWorkWebWeight).
why: Measured in a played town: an older-work effect of +0.3 (a 30% change in the researched outcome) moved the share of 62 to 67 year olds at work from 0.656 to 0.677, about 3%, because the choice scores are logistic and the entry and exit pulls are small.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A weight on the term, fitted in a played year so each group's share moves by the researched size (mothers, married women), as jobsOlderWorkWebWeight is for ages 62 to 66.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: defense-contracts-to-earnings does nothing: its cause federal.defense-boost-pct (extra defense contracts as a share of the state's output) is not recorded by any engine, so the link never runs; the pay level already reads labor.median-earnings and will carry it once the cause exists.
why: No federal procurement engine records state contract awards.
replacement: A federal spending engine recording each state's defense contract awards, read as federal.defense-boost-pct.
resolution: The budgets module records the federal national defense line, and defenseBoostPct (src/core2/gov-measures.ts) reads it above its base, as a share, times the state's fiscal 2024 defense contracts per resident over its output per resident (data/research/federal/defense-contracts-by-state-fy2024.json), read by the web as federal.defense-boost-pct (reader defense-boost-pct, src/core2/modules/outcome-web.ts). The link runs, and the jobs engine's pay level (payLevel in src/core2/modules/jobs.ts) multiplies by its labor.median-earnings factor when it prices an opening and when it raises a worker, shown in law-wiring-labor-web.test.ts.

whatItFakes: minimum-wage-to-low-wage-jobs and federal-minimum-wage-to-low-wage-jobs scale only the staffing targets of employers the jobs engine reviews, and in played towns none of those has a job under the line; the town's low-wage jobs belong to organizations the review never reaches, so the factor moves no record.
why: In a bench world (Sail Harbor, Connecticut, seed 6bad944e1a974146) all 32 reviewed employers had no heads under the line while about 190 of the town's 208 low-wage jobs sat with organizations outside the employers table; summed staffing need was identical to 15 digits with the factor at 0.5.
replacement: The jobs engine applies the low-wage factor to every organization whose jobs labor.low-wage-jobs counts, at the moment it sets that organization's staffing, shown in a low-wage-only twin by employer id.
resolution: Deleted lowWageStaffFactor. A higher wage floor reaches low-wage jobs as pay (wage-floor engine: 213 pay-change records in Higganum CT, 1350 in Attleboro MA, 61 in Marcola OR) and reaches staffing and prices through the employers' own books: in a twin pair in Attleboro MA (seed bc7595dd..., floor 1500 -> 2251, 13 months past the law) yearly payroll rose from $48,983,047 to $59,528,919, the mean price index from 1.0284 to 1.0359 and jobs at firms moved from 1215 to 1210, with 62 firms open in both (scripts/world-proofs/minimum-wage-twin.ts). labor.low-wage-jobs stays a measure.

whatItFakes: A town resident's regional job is priced from the BLS OEWS wage for the occupation of the town role nearest to what they were paid (metro or state area, starting percentile, moved with the place's pay level). The seeker row now keeps the person's last job (lastJob), but it is read only where the town has no role to copy; otherwise the town role's occupation, not the person's own, sets the wage. Where OEWS publishes no wage for the occupation, the town's own nearest role sets the pay.
why: The seeker row keeps only the last pay, not the occupation of the last job, so the occupation is taken from the town role nearest in pay.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Keep the occupation of the last job on the seeker row and price the regional job from it.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: Town workers are let go at a fixed pace (the JOLTS layoff rate, moved by the state's unemployment, age and traits) instead of by their employers' own books and demand. A firm's demand does not shake month to month the way real firms' does (a big customer lost, a contract ended, a bad season), so without this pull the town's firms almost never separate anyone.
why: Measured Nov 8 with the pull switched off (24 months, scripts/world-proofs/jobs-24-months.ts, main 48561f2a): Algiers VT 5001035 r7 unemployment 0.2% mean with 0 layoffs and 0 hires in months 12 and 24; Utah place 4906590 n8b 0.0%, 23 zero months; North Carolina place 3755940 rnd-a 0.0%, 24 zero months; Clinton CT 0915420 r7 0.8% mean. With it: 2.3%, 1.1%, 0.5% and 4.9% and 6 to 15 layoffs a year in a 100-worker town. Deleting the pull removes the labor market's churn, not a target. Measured Nov 9 with the national cycle on main (1366972d4e) and the pull switched off (24 months, scripts/world-proofs/jobs-24-months.ts, seed r7, branch jobs/regional-no-employer): Algiers VT 5001035 has 0 layoffs in months 6, 12, 18 and 24 and holds 4-7% out of work on the opening cohort and entrants alone (with the pull 8-11%); place 1576584 has 0 to 2 layoffs a month and 0.9-3.9% (with the pull 4.6-7%). The cycle moves every firm by one place factor, so it supplies recessions and no idiosyncratic separations. The pull is sized at the CPS employment-to-unemployment flow (pastWorkLayoffsPerQuarter 0.029, FRED LNS17400000). Spread over seven draws (Nov 9, 24 months, Algiers VT 5001035, branch jobs/regional-no-employer), out of work at month 24: r7 10.6% (8-11% in year 2), r8 8.1%, r9 4.8%, r10 5.6%, r11 5.3%, r12 4.3%, r13 4.5% (mean 6.2%, median 5.3%); a 130-worker town moves 0.7% a person, so read it as a spread. Clinton CT 0915420 2.7-4.4% and place 4103650 2.5-3.8% (seed r7) are in range.
replacement: Firm-level demand shocks that come from the world's own records (a customer household or firm that moves, closes, loses income or changes suppliers; a contract that ends; the season), read by the employer's staffing review (reviewEmployers: observedStaff against projected). Plan (Coordinator, Nov 8): a fractional drop in demand cuts hours first, as a sliding scale, with pay and the household's money following; whole-head separations come from discrete causes in the firm's own records (cash running out and the firm closing, the owner's age or health and a retirement or sale, a worker quitting for a better regional job, a worker's own life events). One PR each: hours, then each discrete cause. Then delete reviewTurnover and its pull table. Evidence Nov 8 that jobs-only changes do not lift the small-town flat line (24 months, scripts/world-proofs/jobs-24-months.ts, mean out-of-work share and zero months): Utah place 4906590 n8b is 0.6% with 17 zero months on main and with the age-aware find (#7720); raising jobsQuitBaseline to -2.5 left it at 0.5% and 17 zero months and took Clinton CT 0915420 r7 from 2.5% to 7.6% (peak 15.7%), and at -2.3 to 14.0%; sending a counted quitter through the entry review as a full person who left work left Utah at 17 zero months, NC 3755940 rnd-a at 15, and made Clinton erratic (13 zero months, 12% peak). The cause is upstream of the jobs engine: about 80% of a small town's firm sales are outside buyers who follow one smooth place factor (macro.ts publishConditions), so no firm's demand diverges; firm-level shocks wait on Money's national cycle and on hours cuts through api.rehourJob (#7719), then the discrete causes (closure when cash runs out, owner retirement or sale). Needs firm-level demand that differs between sellers in a town: the outside buyers' sales (about 80% of a small town's firm sales) divided among its sellers by price, capacity and quality (src/core2/residents-economy.ts scaleOutsideSales and the business engine), so a firm that raises prices on a wage rise or a new competitor loses sales for its own recorded reasons.

whatItFakes: How finding work slows with age is one elasticity (0.4 above age 40) fitted to two unverified BLS age bands (55-64 mean 25.0 weeks, 65 and over 29.8) and the all-ages mean (FRED UEMPMEAN); the 16-54 bands are not on file.
why: bls.gov refuses the cloud container (403) and web.archive.org resets, so BLS table cpsaat31 (unemployed by age and duration) could not be read; the Coordinator ruled Nov 8: estimate, never unknown.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: BLS CPS table cpsaat31 (mean and median weeks by age band) read into data/research/labor/ and fitted band by band.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: The opening's seekers use each age band's unemployment ratio from the nation's labor force (CPS) scaled so its mean over the town's own workers is one; the region's rate already holds the county's own age mix, so the scaling should use the county's worker age mix, which the opening does not read. A town older than its county therefore opens at the county's rate, not somewhat below it.
why: The county's worker age mix is not in the regional series the opening reads (state and county labor statistics). Before the scaling, Douglas, Michigan (2622740) opened with 17 seekers where the county's 4.72% implies 22 to 24, because 37% of its counted working-age jobs sit in the fifth age band (ratio 0.73); with the town-mix scaling it opens 20.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Scale the band ratios so their job-weighted mean is one over the county's age mix of workers (ACS), then apply them to the town's mix; a town older than its county then opens below the county only by how much older it is.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: A vacancy's wait before it can be filled depends on the firm's industry only (JOLTS openings over hires). Davis, Faberman and Haltiwanger show vacancy duration also varies with the establishment's size and growth; the firm's size is not read.
why: The industry series is the published figure; a size gradient needs establishment-size microdata not fetched tonight.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Scale each firm's duration by the size gradient of DHI's hires-per-vacancy rate once the establishment-size table is sourced.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.

whatItFakes: The ban-the-box twin-world proof (src/core2/jobs-record-bias.test.ts) gives half of the town's laid-off seekers a conviction by writing a case and a sentence into the justice tables as the justice engine writes them. The laid-off seekers, the funded police opening and the ranking are played; the convictions are not, because the played justice engine convicts only after a bribery investigation and a drawn town rarely produces one in the months a proof runs.
why: The justice engine convicts through investigations of bribery and the cases they bring; ordinary crime in the world does not yet end in a conviction record for a named resident, so a resident with a record who looks for work does not arise in a played year.
replacement: Ordinary crime, arrest and trial in the justice engine ending in convictions for named residents, so the proof draws a place where a resident with a record applies and uses that person.

whatItFakes: The penalty an employer puts on an applicant with a conviction, and the ban-the-box law that lifts it, are read only for public employers in the town and only for full (named) applicants. Private employers are not read even where the state's law covers them (California, Connecticut, Colorado and others), and a counted seeker has no personal record to weigh, though the justice engine keeps counted cases. The penalty is one ESTIMATED number for every public employer.
why: The justice engine keeps a conviction per named person (convictionsOf) but a counted seeker's record is a count by case, not an applicant's; whether a private employer is covered is in the state row's note, not a field the jobs engine reads.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Read the state row's private-employer coverage for private employers, and a counted seeker's share with a record from the justice engine's counted cases, by the same rule as a full person; size the penalty from the callback gap by employer type.
resolution: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage; too in depth, owner): the player sees nothing of the difference; the estimate stays.
